correctness.rationale: Hypergeometric selection of exactly one member of each species gives the established exact expectation. The all-N one-unit-transfer difference has generating polynomial (1+z)^(N-a)Q(z); Q has one positive-to-negative coefficient transition from monotone binomial ratios, and repeated (1+z) convolution cannot increase the number. Endpoint coefficients force exactly one. For N<=17 all partitions and same-length strictly majorized ordered pairs are exhaustively classified in exact integer arithmetic by two independent partition generation methods, with full 2^17 labeled-subset checks for each of the unique witness profiles. The finite cutoff is exhaustively proved only in the stated class; no finite experiment is used as an infinite proof.

broader_coverage.reasoning: A theorem that orders total observed richness under majorization is not a theorem about the singleton frequency coordinate: a category can cease to be singleton when a second member is sampled, and the category count is not monotone in subset inclusion. Frequency-of-frequencies first-moment identities allow the computations but do not entail the local sign-variation lemma or the sharp finite minimum without substantial new arguments.

originality.rationale: Existing literature covers the singleton expectation formula and known ecological applications, so those are not claimed as new. Inspected directly relevant full texts and distinct known results do not imply the novel local sign-variation theorem or the sharp, unique global majorization triple-reversal boundary at N=17. Actual research-index queries were compared for equivalent names, larger parameter ranges and numerical tables. A residual possibility of an unindexed equivalent majorization/frequency-of-frequencies theorem persists.
residual_risks: No independent full bibliographic audit: other work on total positivity, ecological majorization, or occupancy frequency spectra may contain an equivalent theorem with different wording.

value.rationale: The sample-singleton frequency is a principal ecological occupancy statistic, used in sample-completeness assessment. The one-unit-transfer generating-polynomial law is general across every finite census and explains a structural single-switch restriction. The exact 17-individual classification pinpoints the first failure of that seemingly natural restriction under majorization, and the unique triple-reversal witness is a concrete boundary requiring more than a single transfer. This is a meaningful comparison between local balancing and global majorization and not an arbitrary numerical slice; no claims about empirical ecological outcomes are made.
